newsitem.title: USA: Peru's Fujimori says Shining Path has no future.
newsitem.headline: Peru's Fujimori says Shining Path has no future.

text.p: Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori said on Friday his country's Maoist Shining Path rebels had no future despite its successful car bomb attack this week.

Fujimori, on his first visit to the United States since Peruvian troops ended the four-month siege of the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima on April 22, said the blast on Thursday was an isolated incident.

The bombing in Lima injured at least eight police officers and was "an isolated case that could happen in any country in the world," Fujimori told reporters after a speech to the Council on Foreign Relations in New York.
He suggested that the Shining Path, which fought police in a poor Lima neighbourhood before setting the bomb off near a police station, was fighting a lost cause.
"This doesn't mean the Shining Path has any chances left. The government is working so that this kind of thing can be eliminated little by little," he said.

According to a Peruvian police document, the Shining Path has warned it would mark May with attacks as a way to retake the initiative after being overshadowed by the leftist Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA).

MRTA guerrillas jumped into the world headlines by seizing the Japanese ambassador's home in December and holding scores of high-ranking officials and prominent businessmen hostage. The guerrillas had demanded the release of jailed comrades.
Shining Path was weakened by the 1992 capture of its leader but has been regrouping in the last year. It remains stronger than the MRTA.
Fujimori is on a five-day private trip to the United States that will include a stop in Boston to attend his eldest daughter's college graduation on Sunday.
He brushed off a question about Lori Berenson, an American jailed for life by a Peruvian military court last year after being convicted for conspiring with the MRTA.
"We really hope that there is a change of attitude by those who believed that the MRTA was a group of simple guerrillas," he said, adding that Berenson had belonged to the group.
The Clinton administration has repeatedly called for a non-military re-trial of the 28-year-old Berenson, whose parents live in New York.

Fujimori, 58, who underwent an operation on Sunday on his mouth, said he was feeling better but was having trouble speaking clearly. Doctors at Lima's top cancer hospital said tissue removed from his mouth was benign.
